provenance.method: lesson notes written from the NERDC 2025 scheme of work outline; every week keeps its scheme topic and bullets as the teaching spine

topics.title: Revision of jss two work
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to list the states of matter, explain energy transformation with examples, and solve simple problems on energy conversion.

Introduction:
Today we will revise what we learned in JSS Two about matter and energy. These are fundamental concepts that build our understanding of science.

Content:
Matter exists in three states: solid, liquid and gas. For example, stone is solid, water is liquid, and air is gas. Energy cannot be created or destroyed but can change forms. When you cook with a kerosene stove, chemical energy changes to heat energy. Work is done when force moves an object. If you push a danfo bus and it moves, you have done work.

Class activity:
Students will work in groups to identify examples of matter in different states and energy transformations in everyday activities around the school.

Evaluation questions:
1. Name the three states of matter.
2. Give one example of energy transformation.
3. What is work in scientific terms?
4. How is matter different from energy?

Summary:
Understanding matter and energy helps us explain many phenomena in our daily lives and forms the basis for more complex scientific concepts.

topics.title: Family health: genes and traits
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to define genes and traits, differentiate between dominant and recessive traits, and construct a simple family tree showing inherited traits.

Introduction:
We have learned about living things in previous classes. Today we will explore how characteristics are passed from parents to children through genes.

Content:
Genes are units of heredity that we inherit from our parents. They determine our traits like height, eye color, and hair texture. Some traits are dominant while others are recessive. A dominant trait will show up even if only one gene is present, like broad hairline in many Nigerian families. A recessive trait only shows when two genes are present, like attached earlobes. In a family, children can inherit a mix of traits from both parents.

Class activity:
Students will interview family members about visible traits like hair type, eye color, and widow's peak to construct their own family trees showing inheritance patterns.

Evaluation questions:
1. What are genes?
2. Distinguish between dominant and recessive traits.
3. Give an example of a dominant trait.
4. Why do siblings look different even when they have the same parents?

Summary:
Understanding how traits are inherited helps us appreciate the diversity within families and explains why we resemble some relatives more than others.

topics.title: Environmental health
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to identify different types of waste, explain how improper waste disposal leads to disease, and suggest ways to improve school sanitation.

Introduction:
Our environment affects our health directly. We have learned about living things and their needs. Today we will see how waste in our environment can cause diseases.

Content:
Waste is any material that is no longer needed. There are solid waste like plastic bottles and food scraps, liquid waste like dirty water, and gaseous waste from smoke. When waste is not properly disposed of, it becomes a breeding ground for disease-causing organisms. For example, stagnant water in gutters around market stalls can breed mosquitoes that cause malaria. Harmattan season brings dust that can carry germs if waste is left exposed. Poor sanitation can lead to cholera, typhoid, and other diseases.

Class activity:
Students will conduct a sanitation audit of the school compound, identifying waste disposal problems and suggesting solutions.

Evaluation questions:
1. List three types of waste.
2. How does improper waste disposal lead to disease?
3. Name two diseases caused by poor environmental sanitation.
4. What can students do to improve sanitation in our school?

Summary:
Maintaining a clean environment is essential for preventing diseases and promoting good health in our communities.

topics.title: Micro organisms
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to classify microorganisms as useful or harmful, name examples of each, and identify conditions that promote their growth.

Introduction:
We have learned about living things and their environments. Today we will study microorganisms that are too small to be seen with the naked eye but have big impacts on our lives.

Content:
Microorganisms are tiny living things like bacteria, fungi, and viruses. Some are useful while others are harmful. Useful microorganisms help in making foods like yam flour (elubo) and fufu. They also help in decay and composting. Harmful microorganisms cause diseases like malaria and cholera. Fungi like mold grow on bread left in humid weather. Bacteria can spoil food like beans and rice if not stored properly. Microorganisms grow well in warm, moist conditions and dirty environments.

Class activity:
Students will observe different types of mold growing on bread samples kept in various conditions (light, dark, dry, moist) and record their findings.

Evaluation questions:
1. What are microorganisms?
2. Give one example of a useful microorganism.
3. Name one disease caused by harmful microorganisms.
4. What conditions promote the growth of microorganisms?

Summary:
Microorganisms are all around us and play important roles in our environment, food production, and health.

topics.title: Diseases and prevention
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to define communicable diseases, list common examples, and explain methods of prevention including immunization.

Introduction:
In our previous lesson, we learned about microorganisms that can cause diseases. Today we will focus on how these diseases spread and how we can protect ourselves from them.

Content:
Communicable diseases are illnesses that can spread from person to person through air, water, food, or physical contact. Examples include malaria spread by mosquito bites, cholera from contaminated water, and measles through the air. Prevention is better than cure. We can prevent diseases by keeping our environment clean, drinking boiled or treated water, eating well-cooked food, and getting immunized. Immunization is when we are given vaccines to protect us from specific diseases like polio and tuberculosis.

Class activity:
Students will create immunization charts showing recommended vaccines for different age groups and their importance in preventing diseases.

Evaluation questions:
1. What are communicable diseases?
2. Name three ways communicable diseases can spread.
3. Explain the importance of immunization.
4. How can keeping our environment clean help prevent diseases?

Summary:
Preventing communicable diseases requires good personal hygiene, environmental sanitation, and timely immunization.

topics.title: The circulatory system
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to identify the main components of blood, explain the function of the heart, and demonstrate how exercise affects pulse rate.

Introduction:
We have learned about different body systems. Today we will explore the circulatory system that transports substances around the body.

Content:
The circulatory system consists of the heart, blood vessels, and blood. Blood has four components: red blood cells that carry oxygen, white blood cells that fight germs, platelets that help clot blood, and plasma that carries nutrients. The heart pumps blood to all parts of the body. When you exercise like running or playing football, your heart beats faster to supply more oxygen to your muscles. You can feel your pulse by pressing your fingers on your wrist or neck. The pulse rate is the number of heartbeats per minute.

Class activity:
Students will measure their pulse rate at rest and after different exercises (jumping rope, running in place) and record the changes.

Evaluation questions:
1. Name the four components of blood.
2. What is the function of the heart?
3. How does exercise affect pulse rate?
4. Where can you find your pulse?

Summary:
The circulatory system is vital for transporting oxygen, nutrients, and waste products throughout the body to keep us healthy.

topics.title: The nervous system
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to explain reflex actions, identify parts of the nervous system, and measure reaction time in different situations.

Introduction:
We have studied how the body moves and responds. Today we will learn about the nervous system that controls these responses.

Content:
The nervous system consists of the brain, spinal cord, and nerves. It controls all body activities. A reflex action is a quick, automatic response to a stimulus without thinking. For example, when you touch a hot stove, you pull your hand away immediately before your brain processes the pain. The brain is the control center that thinks and remembers. The spinal cord connects the brain to all body parts. Nerves carry messages between the brain and different parts of the body.

Class activity:
Students will work in pairs to test reaction time using a ruler drop test and compare reaction times with and without distractions.

Evaluation questions:
1. What is a reflex action?
2. Name the three main parts of the nervous system.
3. Give an example of a reflex action.
4. How does the nervous system help us survive?

Summary:
The nervous system allows us to respond quickly to our environment and coordinate all body functions.

topics.title: Metabolism in the body
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to define metabolism, explain the role of enzymes in digestion, and demonstrate how enzymes work in a simple experiment.

Introduction:
We have learned about different body systems that work together. Today we will focus on how the body processes food for energy through metabolism.

Content:
Metabolism is all the chemical reactions that happen in our bodies to convert food into energy. Enzymes are special proteins that speed up these reactions. In digestion, enzymes break down food into smaller molecules that can be absorbed. For example, the enzyme amylase in saliva breaks down starch into sugars. Different enzymes work in different parts of the digestive system. Without enzymes, digestion would be too slow to sustain life.

Class activity:
Students will conduct an experiment using amylase enzyme on starch solution, testing for the presence of sugar at different time intervals to observe digestion.

Evaluation questions:
1. What is metabolism?
2. What are enzymes and what do they do?
3. Name one enzyme and its function.
4. Why are enzymes important for digestion?

Summary:
Metabolism and enzymes work together to convert food into energy and building materials that our bodies need to function properly.

topics.title: Drugs and substance abuse
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to define drugs and substance abuse, list effects of drug abuse, and practice refusal skills for peer pressure.

Introduction:
As young adults, you will face choices about substances that can affect your health. Today we will learn about drugs and how to make healthy choices.

Content:
Drugs are substances that change how the body works. When used properly, some drugs like medicines can cure diseases. Substance abuse is when drugs are used in ways that are harmful. Effects of drug abuse include health problems like liver damage, mental issues, and addiction. Peer pressure can lead to substance abuse. Learning to say no is important skills. You can refuse by giving reasons, suggesting alternatives, or walking away. Many Nigerian organizations run say no campaigns to help youth resist drug pressure.

Class activity:
Students will create posters and role-play scenarios demonstrating effective ways to refuse drugs and other harmful substances when offered by peers.

Evaluation questions:
1. What is substance abuse?
2. List two effects of drug abuse.
3. How can you say no to drugs when friends offer them?
4. Why is it important to avoid substance abuse?

Summary:
Making informed choices about substances and developing refusal skills are important for maintaining good health and achieving future goals.

topics.title: Revision and BECE practice
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to answer past BECE questions correctly, identify common exam question patterns, and apply knowledge from the term's topics.

Introduction:
As we approach the end of the term, we will revise all topics we have covered and practice examination questions to prepare for the BECE.

Content:
We will review key concepts from each topic including matter and energy, family health, environmental health, microorganisms, diseases, circulatory system, nervous system, metabolism, and drugs. Special attention will be given to definitions, examples, and relationships between concepts. We will practice past BECE questions to familiarize students with the format and requirements. Students will learn to read questions carefully, identify what is being asked, and provide concise answers that address all parts of the question.

Class activity:
Students will work in groups to solve past BECE questions, mark each other's work, and discuss areas of difficulty.

Evaluation questions:
1. Explain how genes determine traits.
2. Describe how the circulatory system works.
3. What are the effects of environmental pollution on health?
4. How do microorganisms affect our daily lives?
5. Design a simple experiment to test enzyme activity.

Summary:
Regular revision and practice with past questions are essential for success in examinations and for retaining scientific knowledge.
